title: Market research
examples: What is the difference between primary and secondary data?
When should I use a sample instead of a whole population?
Can you give an example of a good sampling technique?

explain.say: Today we are learning about market research methods. This helps businesses understand customers. We will look at two main types of data sources.
Primary research means gathering new information yourself. You are collecting data directly from the source. Think about asking people questions in person.
Secondary research uses data that already exists somewhere. This saves time and money for the business. Examples include census data or old studies.
When studying a large group, we often use sampling. This means studying a small group that represents the whole. It is much easier and quicker this way.
For example, if you want to know about all students in a school, you cannot ask everyone. You might survey one class to represent the whole school.
In real life, a new mobile phone company needs to know what features people want. They will run surveys to gather primary data. They might also check old sales reports for secondary data.

faq.q: What is the main difference between primary and secondary research?
faq.a: Primary research means collecting brand new data yourself. Secondary research means using information that someone else has already collected.

faq.q: When is it better to use a sample instead of the whole population?
faq.a: It is better when the population is too large or too spread out to collect data from everyone. Sampling makes the research manageable.
asks: Do I always need a sample?

faq.q: Can I use online sources for secondary research?
faq.a: Yes, many websites and online databases provide secondary data. Always check if the source is reliable and trustworthy.
asks: Are websites good for secondary data?

faq.q: Does the size of the sample affect the results?
faq.a: Yes, generally, a larger sample size gives results that are closer to the true population value. However, the sampling method matters more.
asks: Is a big sample always better?

faq.q: What is the best way to choose a sample?
faq.a: The best way depends on the research question. Sometimes random selection is best, but sometimes specific groups are needed.
asks: How do I pick my sample?
What is a good sampling technique?

facts: Primary data is gathered directly by the researcher.
Secondary data can come from government reports or academic journals.
Sampling is used when studying a population too large to survey entirely.
A sample must accurately represent the entire population.

quiz.say: A company reviews last year's national sales statistics to plan next year's marketing.
quiz.why: The data already exists in past reports, so it is secondary.

wrong.0: Sampling is a method of selection, not the source of the data itself.
wrong.2: This would mean they are collecting brand new data, not reviewing old records.
wrong.3: This refers to the whole group, not the type of data source used.

quiz.say: A student interviews ten local shop owners about their business challenges.
quiz.why: The student is gathering new, firsthand information directly from the owners.

wrong.0: Secondary research uses data that already exists somewhere else.
wrong.1: This implies surveying every single owner, which is not what the student is doing.
wrong.2: Sampling is the technique used; the act of interviewing is the type of research.

quiz.say: A market researcher wants to know about all university students in a large city. They decide to survey only students from three specific colleges.
quiz.why: They are using a small, manageable group (the colleges) to represent the whole city population.

wrong.0: They are actively collecting new data through surveys, not using old reports.
wrong.1: While it involves new data, the core concept here is reducing the scope from all students to a manageable few.
wrong.2: A population study would require surveying all students in the entire city.
